issues.legal_issue: The succession route for a woman’s holding depends on whether her title originated in inheritance from a male predecessor or in an independent interest of her own.
material_facts: The woman continued in possession of a tenancy after her husband died, as his heir under the law then in force.
Later tenancy legislation conferred statutory-tenant, hereditary-tenant and bhumidhar status on her, but those changes did not alter the inherited origin of her title.
After her death, her married daughter and her husband’s brother’s son claimed the holding; the succession order applicable at the time preferred the brother’s son.
issues.conclusion: The woman had inherited an interest from her husband, so succession was governed by Section 172 read with Section 171, not Section 174. The holding devolved to the husband’s brother’s son in preference to the married daughter.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 172 and 171 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 apply where a woman’s interest originated in inheritance from her husband; Section 174 applies where she held an independent interest of her own. The words “inherited an interest” encompass even a limited or precarious interest, and later statutory changes in the form or status of that interest do not change the origin of title. Section 48 of the Oudh Rent Act, 1886 recognized the heir’s limited right to retain occupation, supporting the conclusion that the woman’s interest came by inheritance. The Court approved Mst. Jaini v. Ram Prasad, A.I.R. 1952 All. 852.

predicates.female_holder_succession_dispute: A dispute arose over who succeeds to a holding after a female holder died.
predicates.interest_originated_in_inheritance_from_: The female holder first obtained her interest in the holding as an heir of a male predecessor.
predicates.later_legal_status_did_not_change_title_: Later laws conferred new tenancy or landholding statuses on the female holder without changing the inherited origin of her title.
predicates.preferred_collateral_heir_competes_with_: A collateral heir in the male predecessor’s family claimed the holding against the female holder’s daughter.
predicates.applicable_succession_order_favors_colla: The succession order applicable when the female holder died ranked the collateral heir ahead of the daughter.

issues.definition: When a female holder’s interest came by inheritance from a male predecessor and later legal changes did not alter that origin, the holding passes under the applicable succession order for that predecessor’s line.

issues.legal_issue: A succession amendment that took effect after the holder’s death does not govern succession to the holder’s estate.
material_facts: The female holder died before the amendment to the land reform legislation took effect.
The parties disputed who succeeded to her holding.
issues.conclusion: The later amendment had no application, and succession was governed by the provisions in force when the holder died.
issues.legal_principle: Section 172-A was introduced by an amendment in 1954, after the holder’s death. It therefore did not apply; succession was governed by Section 172 or Section 174 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, according to the origin of the holder’s interest.

predicates.female_holder_succession_dispute: A dispute arose over who succeeds to a holding after a female holder died.
predicates.holder_died_before_later_amendment_took_: The holder died before a later amendment affecting succession took effect.

issues.definition: If a female holder died before a later amendment took effect, that amendment does not govern the succession dispute.

issues.legal_issue: A Division Bench must follow an earlier Division Bench’s decision on the same legal point, or refer the matter to a larger bench before departing from it, regardless of whether the earlier decision arose in an appeal or the later proceeding is a writ matter.
material_facts: An earlier Division Bench had decided the relevant legal point in an appeal.
A later Division Bench considered the same legal point in a writ proceeding and declined to follow the earlier decision because it arose in an appeal.
issues.conclusion: The earlier Division Bench’s ratio was binding despite the different procedural forms; the later Division Bench could not disregard it and should have referred the matter to a larger bench if it wished to differ.
issues.legal_principle: The rule of judicial precedent binds a Division Bench to the ratio of an earlier Division Bench on the same point, regardless of whether the earlier decision arose in an appeal or the later matter is a writ proceeding. A Bench wishing to differ must refer the matter to a larger bench. The Court rejected the later Bench’s treatment of Mst. Jaini v. Ram Prasad, A.I.R. 1952 All. 852, as distinguishable solely because it had been decided in an appeal.

predicates.later_division_bench_proceeding: A Division Bench later considered a legal point in a proceeding before it.
predicates.earlier_coordinate_bench_decided_same_le: An earlier Division Bench had decided the same legal point.
predicates.procedural_form_is_different: The earlier and later proceedings had different procedural forms.

issues.definition: When a later Division Bench encounters the same legal point decided by an earlier Division Bench, a difference in procedural form does not permit it to disregard that decision; it must follow it or refer the matter to a larger bench.
